0.title: Amazing Grace from First to Last
0.essay:
The Bible ends with one word of blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen” (Revelation 22:21). After sixty-six books of creation, fall, law, prophets, gospel and promise, the last thing God says to his people is “grace”. It is a fitting end, because grace runs through the whole story.

What grace is

Grace is God’s free, undeserved favour toward people who deserve the opposite. A simple way to remember it: mercy is God not giving us what we deserve; grace is God giving us what we do not deserve. We deserve judgment, and he gives forgiveness, adoption, the Holy Spirit, a new heart and eternal life. He gives all of it freely, at his own cost, in Jesus Christ.

Easy to say, hard to believe

Every human heart leans toward earning. We want to deserve God’s favour, or at least to contribute something. That instinct produces two opposite errors. One is legalism, which tries to earn God’s acceptance by keeping rules. The other is licence, which treats grace as permission to sin. Both misunderstand grace. Scripture shows a grace that saves without our works and then trains us to live for God.

This study follows the historic Reformed understanding: salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and God’s saving grace does not merely make salvation possible but actually brings his people to faith and keeps them to the end. Where Christians differ on that, the main views are set out fairly.

The chapters

What Grace Is; The God of All Grace in the Old Testament; Saving Grace; Grace Against Legalism and Licence; Grace for Every Day; and Growing in Grace and Showing Grace. It belongs with the studies on the Holiness of God and the Fear of the Lord. Only those who see how holy God is will see how amazing his grace is.

1.title: What Grace Is
1.essay:
The clearest definition of grace in the Bible comes in one sentence: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Every phrase excludes us

Not your own doing. A gift. Not of works. No boasting. Faith is the hand that receives the gift, not a work that earns it. And the purpose is plain: “so that no one may boast”. In heaven no one will say, “I made the right choice,” or “I was more spiritual than others.” Everyone will say, “It was all grace.” That is why grace humbles us and fills us with joy at the same time.

The opposite of wages

“Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due” (Romans 4:4). If we could earn salvation, God would owe it to us. But grace is never owed. And grace and works cannot be mixed: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Romans 11:6).

That verse is a logical knife. Grace with a little bit of works is like a gift with a small invoice attached; it is no longer a gift. Many people believe that God helps those who help themselves, or that grace makes up the difference after we have done our best. Paul will have none of it. Either grace saves completely, or it does not save at all.

For the ungodly

Grace is not God’s favour to good people, or even to people who are trying. It is favour to the ungodly. Paul contrasts the one who works and receives wages with the one who “does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). Not the nearly good or the improving, but the ungodly. “But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Grace does not find us worthy; it makes us accepted. And this was always God’s way: Abraham himself was counted righteous by faith (Romans 4:3).

Grace is a person

Grace is not a substance God pours into us or a force in the universe. It is God himself turning toward us in kindness, and it comes to us in a person. “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). “For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1:16) — one gift piled on another, wave after wave without end. “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). The law was good, but it could only show God’s standard. Christ brings what the law never could. To receive grace is to receive Christ.

Free to us, costly to God

Grace and mercy are close companions. Mercy is God’s compassion toward the miserable and guilty, withholding the punishment they deserve; grace is his favour toward the undeserving, giving the blessing they could never earn. In Christ we receive both.

Grace is free to us, but it was not cheap. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Every gift of grace was purchased by the Son of God.

And it did not begin when we believed. God saved us “because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (2 Timothy 1:9). It goes back to eternity, and it ends in glory: God saves by grace “to the praise of his glorious grace” (Ephesians 1:6). If we contributed to our salvation, we would share the glory. Because it is all of grace, all the glory goes to God, and that is our deepest joy too.

The thief and the churchgoer

One of the criminals crucified beside Jesus had no time to reform his life, be baptised, go to church or do good works. He simply turned to Jesus and said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Jesus answered, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). He is the clearest picture in the Gospels of salvation by grace alone.

A man raised in church has quietly believed for years that God accepts him because he is a decent person: he attends, he gives, he avoids the obvious sins. When he finally understands Ephesians 2, it is both humbling and liberating. Humbling, because his goodness counts for nothing in his salvation. Liberating, because he no longer has to keep up the performance. For the first time, he rests.

Finish this sentence honestly: “God accepts me because…” If anything after “because” is about you — your faithfulness, your effort, your goodness — you have not yet fully grasped grace. The only true answer is, “because of Jesus Christ.”

For reflection

How would you explain the difference between grace and mercy to a child? Why does the human heart resist grace so strongly? Read Ephesians 2:1–10: which phrase about grace strikes you most? How did you finish the sentence “God accepts me because…”, and what does your answer reveal?

2.title: The God of All Grace in the Old Testament
2.essay:
Some people imagine that the Old Testament shows a God of law and wrath, and the New Testament a God of grace and love. But the God of the Old Testament describes himself first of all as gracious.

God’s own name

Just after Israel’s sin with the golden calf, when God had every reason to destroy them, Moses asked to see his glory. “The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, ‘The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness’” (Exodus 34:6). This self-description is quoted again and again through the Old Testament (Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Grace comes first and fills the description.

But God also says that he “will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7). His grace never sets his justice aside. So the Old Testament leaves a question hanging: how can God forgive sin and still not clear the guilty? The sacrifices pointed toward the answer, and the cross supplied it. There God forgives the guilty by bearing their guilt himself.

Grace from the beginning

After the fall, God came looking for Adam and Eve, clothed them and promised a Saviour (Genesis 3:15, 21). In a world so corrupt that God resolved to judge it, “Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8). God chose Abraham from a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2). He chose Jacob, a deceiver. He heard Hagar in the desert (Genesis 16:13). And he chose Israel, not because they were impressive: “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8).

The only reason given for God’s love is God’s love. That sounds circular, but it is the deepest comfort. A love that is not caused by our goodness cannot be lost by our failure. God does not choose people because they are impressive; he chooses them, and then makes them something. Paul says the same of the Corinthians: “not many of you were wise according to worldly standards” (1 Corinthians 1:26).

Even the law was grace

Before the Ten Commandments, God said, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Redemption came first, then the law. Israel was not given the law in order to be saved; they were given it because they had been saved.

God has never saved anyone by works. Old Testament believers were saved by grace through faith, looking forward to God’s promised redemption, just as we look back to it. Paul uses Abraham and David as his examples of justification by faith (Romans 4:1–8).

A seat at the king’s table

After Saul’s death, David asked, “Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” (2 Samuel 9:3). The answer was Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, lame in both feet, living in obscurity and probably afraid the new king would kill him as a rival. David said, “Do not fear,” restored everything Saul had lost, and told him, “you shall eat at my table always” (2 Samuel 9:7) — for the sake of his father Jonathan.

The chapter ends by reminding us that Mephibosheth “was lame in both his feet” (2 Samuel 9:13). He never became impressive. He simply ate at the king’s table for the rest of his life. That is a picture of every believer: still weak, still dependent, and always welcome for Christ’s sake.

He will abundantly pardon

When Israel failed again and again, God’s grace persisted. The prophets are full of tender invitations: “let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” (Isaiah 55:7). Micah ends his prophecy with a question that plays on his own name, which means “Who is like the LORD?”: “Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression?” (Micah 7:18). God “delights in steadfast love”. He does not forgive reluctantly. “You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19). Sins thrown into the deepest sea are gone for good; grace does not keep a record, waiting to bring them up again.

Even in the ruins of Jerusalem, Jeremiah could write, “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23). Grace is not a single event but a daily supply.

Jonah’s complaint

Jonah ran from God precisely because he knew God was gracious. He did not want Nineveh forgiven: “for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful” (Jonah 4:2). Sometimes we resent God’s grace to others even while we depend on it ourselves.

A woman reading the Old Testament for the first time expects to find a harsh God. Instead she finds the God who clothes Adam and Eve, hears Hagar, forgives David and pleads with Israel through the prophets. She realises that the God of grace was there all along, and that Jesus is not a different God but the fullest revelation of the same one.

For reflection

Have you ever thought of the Old Testament God as harsh? How does Exodus 34:6–7 challenge that? Read 2 Samuel 9: in what ways are you like Mephibosheth? Why is it a comfort that God’s love is not caused by anything in us? Do you, like Jonah, ever resent God’s grace to others?

3.title: Saving Grace
3.essay:
How does a person come to be saved? Ephesians 2 answers by describing what we were before grace: “And you were dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1). Not sick, not struggling, but dead. And dead people cannot make themselves alive.

But God

Then come two of the most wonderful words in the Bible: “But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:4–5). After three verses of devastating description, everything turns. God acts out of his own character, and he acts while we are dead. He makes us alive, raises us up and seats us with Christ, “so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace” (Ephesians 2:7). Our salvation will display grace for ever. Heaven will never run out of reasons to praise it.

A chain of grace

Saving grace has many parts, and Scripture shows them as a chain. God chose his people in Christ “before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). He sent his Son to redeem them. By his Spirit he calls them, opening their hearts to believe. He justifies them — “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24) — declaring them righteous not on the basis of their righteousness but of Christ’s, received by faith. He adopts them, sanctifies them and will glorify them. “And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Every link is God’s work.

Titus 3 gathers the whole gospel into a few lines. God saved us “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5), “so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:7). The new birth is the beginning, and it is entirely God’s work; the end is an inheritance we could never earn.

Even faith is a gift

Jesus said, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Lydia was a successful businesswoman and a worshipper of God, and she heard Paul preach by the river. Luke tells us exactly why she believed: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul” (Acts 16:14). Paul preached; Lydia listened; but the Lord opened her heart. Faith is truly ours, but it is born of God’s grace. The preacher speaks to the ear; only God can open the heart. That is why prayer must always go with evangelism.

The open door

None of this makes evangelism pointless or the human response unreal. God uses the preaching of the gospel to call his people, and everyone who comes is welcomed. John 6:37 holds both truths together. “All that the Father gives me will come to me”: God’s grace is effective, and those he has given to the Son will certainly come. “And whoever comes to me I will never cast out”: the invitation is open, and no one who comes will be turned away. The first truth assures us that God’s purposes cannot fail; the second gives every sinner a reason to come. No one who comes to Christ need wonder whether they are chosen. Their coming is the evidence.

Can saving grace be resisted?

Christians answer this in two main ways. The Arminian view holds that God gives grace to all people, enabling them to believe, but that each person decides whether to accept or resist it. The Reformed view holds that God’s saving call to his chosen people is effectual: by his Spirit he gives them a new heart, so that they come willingly. Both agree that people are responsible for their unbelief and that the gospel offer is genuine.

The Reformed view is the more likely reading of Scripture. People dead in sin need resurrection, not assistance (Ephesians 2:5). “All that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6:37). And “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48). God does not drag anyone unwilling into his kingdom. He makes the unwilling willing, and so the saved have nothing to boast of.

And the grace that saves also keeps: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). True believers persevere, not because they are strong, but because God’s grace holds them.

Found by grace

Saul of Tarsus was on his way to arrest Christians when the risen Christ stopped him. He was not seeking God; he was fighting him. Later he wrote, “formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13), and he saw his conversion as a pattern, an example “to those who were to believe in him” (1 Timothy 1:16). If grace could save Saul, it can save anyone.

Zacchaeus climbed a tree out of curiosity. Jesus stopped, called him by name and invited himself to his house. By the end of the day Zacchaeus was giving his wealth away, and Jesus said, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). Zacchaeus thought he was looking for Jesus. Jesus was looking for him.

A Christian who prayed for her brother for twenty years wonders whether it was worth it. Then he comes to faith. He cannot explain it, he says: he had heard the gospel many times, but one day it suddenly made sense, and he could not resist it. Her prayers were not wasted. God was at work all along, and his grace was the decisive cause.

For reflection

What does it mean that we were “dead” in sin, and why does that matter for understanding grace? How does knowing that God opens hearts affect the way you pray for and speak to unbelievers? How does John 6:37 hold together God’s sovereignty and the open invitation? Whose conversion are you praying for?

4.title: Grace Against Legalism and Licence
4.essay:
Grace has two great enemies, and they come from opposite directions. One says we must earn God’s favour. The other says that, since we cannot, it does not matter how we live.

Legalism

Legalism says that we must earn God’s acceptance, or keep it, by our performance. It can look very religious. In Galatia, false teachers said that believing in Christ was good, but that Gentile converts also needed circumcision and the law of Moses to be truly accepted. Paul’s response was fierce: “I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (Galatians 2:21). To add anything to Christ is to say his death was not enough. “You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4). Legalism is not a harmless excess of zeal. Paul was willing to confront even Peter publicly when he began to drift toward it (Galatians 2:11–14).

Legalism today rarely looks like circumcision. It looks like believing God loves you more after a good week of devotions; feeling that your standing with God rises and falls with your spiritual performance; adding rules to Scripture and judging others by them; or never being able to rest in forgiveness.

A conscientious believer feels she must earn her way back into God’s favour after she sins. She avoids prayer for a few days, as a kind of penance. Grace tells her to run at once to the throne of grace, because her acceptance rests on Christ, not on her record.

Licence

Licence says that since we are saved by grace, it does not matter how we live. Paul had just written that “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20), and he saw the objection coming: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?” (Romans 6:1–2). His reason is not only that sin is wrong, but that it no longer fits who we are. Believers have been united to Christ in his death and resurrection. Living in sin is like a freed man going back to his prison cell.

Jude warned of people who had crept into the church unnoticed and “who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (Jude 4). The same error is still common: “God is love, so he won’t mind.” Grace that refuses Christ’s lordship is not grace at all.

A young man tells himself that his sexual relationship outside marriage does not matter, because God will forgive him anyway. Grace answers, “By no means!” The grace that forgives also trains us to say no. Someone who uses grace as an excuse to keep sinning should ask whether he has really understood it.

One answer to both

The answer to both errors is the same: a true understanding of grace. Grace saves us completely apart from works, which destroys legalism. And grace transforms us, which destroys licence. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age” (Titus 2:11–12). Grace is not only a pardon; it is a teacher. And it reminds us why Christ died: “to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). Grace does not make people lazy. It makes them zealous.

“For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14). Notice what that means. Being under grace does not give sin more room; it breaks sin’s rule. The law could command but could not change the heart. Grace changes the heart. External rules and rituals cannot; “it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods” (Hebrews 13:9).

Saved for good works

Ephesians 2 says we are saved “not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:9), and then at once that “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). Good works are not the root of salvation but its fruit. We do not work to be saved; we are saved to work.

The moral law of God still shows believers how to love God and neighbour. What changes is our relationship to it. It is no longer a ladder to climb to earn acceptance, but a guide for grateful children who are already accepted.

Two sons

In Jesus’ parable, the younger son wasted everything, came home, and was embraced by his father before he could finish his speech (Luke 15:20–24). But the elder brother refused to join the celebration. He had worked hard and obeyed, and he resented grace given to the undeserving. Both sons were far from the father — one through licence, one through legalism — and the father went out to both.

A congregation slowly develops unwritten rules about clothing, schooling, music and entertainment, and those who do not conform are treated as second-class Christians. Grace calls them back to the essentials of Scripture, and to charity on matters where God has not spoken.

For reflection

Are you more prone to legalism or to licence, and how do you see it in your life? Read Luke 15:11–32: which son do you identify with more, and what does the father teach you? Why does being “under grace” break the dominion of sin? Are there unwritten rules in your church or family that work like legalism?

5.title: Grace for Every Day
5.essay:
Grace is not only how the Christian life begins. It is how it continues. Every day believers live by grace, and God supplies it freely.

Grace for weakness

Paul begged God three times to remove a painful thorn in his flesh (2 Corinthians 12:7–8). God’s answer was “no” to the request and “yes” to something better: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Not “will be”, but “is”: the grace is present now. God is not glorified mainly when strong people do impressive things, but when weak people are held up by his strength. And Paul’s response was remarkable: “Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The thorn was never removed. But he learned to say, “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

A mother of a disabled child prays for years for healing that does not come. She feels guilty for being tired and angry. One day she reads 2 Corinthians 12 and realises that God’s answer to her may be his answer to Paul: not removal, but grace sufficient for each day. Her weakness has not disqualified her. It is where Christ’s power rests.

Grace for need

The throne of God was once the place sinners feared most. Now, because Jesus is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), it has become a throne of grace. “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). We come with confidence, not because we are worthy but because he is: mercy for our failures, grace for our struggles. There is no time of need for which this throne is closed.

Grace for service

Paul knew he did not deserve to be an apostle, having persecuted the church (1 Corinthians 15:9). “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). That is the paradox of Christian effort. Grace does not make us passive. We work hard, and grace gets the credit, because grace was working through our work.

A pastor who has served faithfully for decades is asked what kept him going. He answers that every Sunday he felt inadequate, and every Sunday God gave enough grace. “I have never had grace for next week,” he says, “only for this week.”

Grace for suffering and for the humble

“And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you” (1 Peter 5:10). He is the God of all grace, enough for every kind of trouble.

James wrote to Christians who were quarrelling, envious and worldly, in serious trouble. Yet his first word is hope: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). There is always more grace. The condition for receiving it is not to become better first, but to become humble: to admit our need and come. Grace flows downhill, to the low places. Pride is the only thing that blocks it.

Grace abounding

“And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8). Notice the “all”s. God’s grace is never in short supply. And if he gave us his Son, he will hold back nothing we truly need: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

God ordinarily gives this grace through his word, prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and the fellowship of his church. These are not magic, and they do not save by themselves. But they are the channels through which he has promised to strengthen his people.

Common grace

There is also a wider grace that God shows to everyone, believers and unbelievers alike. “For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). Reformed theology calls this common grace, as distinct from the saving grace given to God’s people in Christ. It restrains evil and gives every good gift in human life — food, friendship, beauty, art, science, family. It explains why unbelievers can be kind, wise and skilled. And it leaves everyone without excuse for not thanking God (Acts 14:17; Romans 1:21).

A Christian enjoys a sunset, a meal with friends and a beautiful piece of music written by an unbeliever. She thanks God for all of it. Common grace teaches her to see his kindness everywhere.

For reflection

Where do you most need to hear “My grace is sufficient for you” right now? How does coming to “the throne of grace” differ from how you usually approach God in prayer? What does 1 Corinthians 15:10 teach about grace and hard work? Where can you see God’s common grace around you this week? Thank him for it.

6.title: Growing in Grace and Showing Grace
6.essay:
Peter’s last words in his last letter are a command: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity” (2 Peter 3:18). We never outgrow grace. We grow into it.

Growing in grace

Grace and knowledge belong together. As we know Christ better, we understand his grace more deeply; as we experience his grace, we know him more truly. And growth in grace always ends in glory for Christ.

We grow through the same means God uses to give grace: by reading and hearing his word, which Paul calls “the word of his grace, which is able to build you up” (Acts 20:32); by prayer at the throne of grace; by the sacraments; and by the fellowship of believers who remind us of the gospel. Growing in grace also means growing in humility, since grace is given to the humble.

Grace received becomes grace given

The New Testament does not ground Christian behaviour in guilt or in the fear of losing God’s love. It grounds it in grace already received. We forgive because we were forgiven, give because Christ gave, and serve because we have been served. Paul appealed to the Corinthians “not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Corinthians 6:1). Grace is meant to bear fruit. Someone who receives grace but never shows it has not yet understood what he has received.

When Barnabas visited the new church at Antioch, “When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad” (Acts 11:23). Grace is visible. Barnabas could see it in changed lives, and it made him rejoice.

In our words

“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). That is a remarkable thought: the grace God gives us can flow through our speech to others. “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6).

A man known for his sharp tongue begins to pray Ephesians 4:29 every morning. He starts noticing how often his words tear down. Slowly, by grace, he learns to encourage his wife, praise his children and speak kindly to difficult colleagues. People say he has mellowed. He knows it is grace.

In forgiveness

Paul names what destroys grace in a community — bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, slander and malice (Ephesians 4:31) — and calls us to the opposite: “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). The measure of our forgiveness is God’s forgiveness of us, and the power for it is his grace in us. People who know how much they have been forgiven become forgivers.

A woman whose husband betrayed her years ago finds she still carries bitterness. She reads Hebrews 12:15: “See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up.” She realises that forgiving does not mean pretending nothing happened, but releasing the debt as God released hers. It takes time, and grace.

In giving

Paul calls the Macedonians’ generosity “the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia” (2 Corinthians 8:1). Raising money for poor believers in Jerusalem, he does not use pressure or guilt. He points to Christ: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). People who have been made rich by Christ’s poverty find it natural to give. Generosity is grace flowing outward.

A couple on a modest income decide to support a missionary family. They cannot give much, but they give gladly. They are learning the grace of giving.

In service

“As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace” (1 Peter 4:10). Peter calls our gifts God’s varied grace — grace in many colours — and calls us stewards, managers of something that belongs to someone else. A church where every member uses their gift is a church where the many-coloured grace of God is on display.

In witness, and to the end

The gospel itself is “the gospel of the grace of God” (Acts 20:24), and Paul counted his life worth nothing compared with testifying to it. Every believer who has received grace is called to make it known.

Paul’s letters almost always begin and end with grace. The Christian life starts in grace, continues in grace and ends in glory, where we will spend eternity discovering “the immeasurable riches of his grace” (Ephesians 2:7).

This week, read Ephesians 2 and Titus 3 slowly. Thank God for one specific grace each day. And as a response to grace, forgive someone, speak a gracious word to someone, and give something away.

For reflection

How has your understanding of grace grown over the years? Read Ephesians 4:25–32: which instruction about speech or forgiveness do you most need to apply? Is there someone you need to forgive “as God in Christ forgave you”? What gift has God entrusted to you, and how could you use it to serve others?
